strengths: Introduces a novel application of test-time training (TTT) as a streaming memory mechanism for long video understanding, with a TTT_MEM layer, a long-span prediction objective, a two-stage training scheme, and a modality-aware memory reading mechanism.

Proposes ELViM, a new benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate long-term episodic memory and procedural knowledge recall from past video experiences, with a careful data creation pipeline to reduce leakage and ensure questions require long-range memory.

Provides extensive experiments on Video-MME, LVBench, VideoEvalPro, StreamingBench, and ELViM, including ablations on memory mechanisms, memory size, frame count, long-span prediction, deepstack embeddings, prediction spans, runtime, and FLOPs.

Demonstrates consistent empirical gains over streaming and non-streaming baselines under matched backbone and training data, especially on ELViM (46.7 vs 38.5/32.5/28.1) and in memory efficiency (TTT_MEM matches similarity merging with less than 25% of the memory tokens).
Reports detailed model architecture, training configurations, hyperparameters, and runtime statistics, which supports reproducibility and practical assessment.
Includes a thoughtful impact statement discussing privacy, bias, and energy risks with mitigation strategies.
weaknesses: Inconsistent numbers between Table 1 and Table 2: Similarity Merging on ELViM is reported as 38.5 in Table 1 but 35.4 in Table 2, with no explanation, undermining confidence in baseline comparisons.

Missing comparisons to several recent streaming video methods mentioned in related work (e.g., ReKV, StreamMem, InfiniPot-V, LiveVLM, VideoChat-Online, OVBench), so the state-of-the-art claim is not fully supported.

No explicit limitations section; important limitations such as audio bypassing TTT_MEM, training at 4 FPS while evaluating at 1 FPS, potential forgetting in fast weights, and benchmark copyright/privacy concerns are not discussed.
The reference list contains numerous errors (e.g., Bai et al. 2018 for 2025 Qwen3-VL/Qwen2.5-VL, inconsistent citation years), reducing scholarly quality and reproducibility.

The TTT_MEM formulation has ambiguities: the meaning of T and the 'Number of Tokens Intervals' in Table 10 is unclear; the update uses an L2 norm without squaring and one SGD step; and the FLOPs table reports only 0.000235 TFLOPs overhead, which appears implausibly small and uses inconsistent units.

ELViM benchmark validation is incomplete: no human accuracy, inter-annotator agreement, or confidence intervals are reported, and questions are generated by Gemini, which may introduce model-specific biases.
The audio-visual claim is under-evaluated: audio tokens bypass TTT_MEM, and no audio-specific ablations or benchmarks are provided despite the model being audio-visual.
Reproducibility is limited: no code or dataset release is stated, and ELViM depends on proprietary model outputs and YouTube videos with potential copyright/privacy issues.

Some claims are overstated: the abstract says 3-7% improvement, but Video-MME long improves by only 1.7% over video-SALMONN 2+; the claimed 15% ELViM improvement is 14.2% against one baseline and 18.6% against another.
Stage 2 training uses up to 2048 frames, while evaluation processes 3-hour videos (3600 frames at 1 FPS), so generalization to much longer streams is not fully validated.

strengths: Proposes video-SALMONN S, the first streaming audio-visual LLM to use test-time training (TTT) as a long-term memory mechanism, with a TTT_MEM layer and a long-span prediction objective.
Introduces the ELViM benchmark for episodic learning from video memory, with a data-creation pipeline designed to avoid knowledge leakage and textual shortcuts.
Reports consistent improvements over strong streaming and non-streaming baselines on multiple long-video benchmarks (Video-MME, LVBench, VideoEvalPro, ELViM, StreamingBench).
Provides ablations on memory size, number of frames, long-span prediction, and alternative memory mechanisms (Mamba-2, TTT-video), showing advantages of TTT_MEM.
Runtime and FLOP analyses suggest TTT_MEM adds negligible computational overhead.
weaknesses: Technical details of TTT_MEM training and the memory-reading mechanism are insufficiently specified. Equations contain mismatched brackets and undefined symbols (e.g., M, m). The memory-reading selection (Eqs. 8–10) appears to keep a fixed m KV pairs rather than an average M, and it is unclear how it satisfies streaming constraints or scales with memory tokens.

The long-span prediction objective (Eq. 3) is questionable: it trains fast weights to reconstruct X_{t-T} from X_t, which may be harmful when chunks are unrelated. The gains are marginal (Table 10: T=2 vs. T=1 differs by 0.7 on Video-MME long and 0.9 on LVBench), and no error bars are reported.

Despite being an audio-visual LLM, the paper does not evaluate audio-visual understanding or ablate the audio modality. Audio tokens are said to bypass TTT_MEM, and no audio-visual benchmarks (e.g., AVQA) are reported, undermining the 'audio-visual' claim.

Reproducibility is poor: no code, model weights, or dataset release; no link to ELViM; missing hyperparameters (loss weighting, inner-loop learning rate, projection dimensions, memory-reading details, data splits). The new benchmark cannot be used by others.

Baselines are limited: only similarity merging (MovieChat), PEMF, Qwen3-VL, and video-SALMONN 2+ are compared. Recent streaming methods (Flash-VStream, Dispider, VideoLLM-online, ReKV, StreamMem, LiveVLM) are discussed but not evaluated, so the SOTA claim is overclaimed.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs. Several improvements are small (e.g., LVBench 55.4 vs. 55.6 with reading; Stage 2 adds only 0.2–0.4). The ELViM benchmark lacks a human performance baseline and inter-annotator agreement.

Presentation is poor: numerous typos, inconsistent notation (video-SALMONN S vs. -S, TTT_MEM vs. TTT_{MEM}), mismatched brackets in equations, and many incorrect reference years/entries (e.g., Qwen3-VL cited as 2018; Chai et al. 2024 for a 2018 paper; Panayotov et al. 2025 for a 2015 paper), making the paper hard to follow and undermining credibility.

No limitations section. The impact statement discusses risks but not methodological limitations, failure modes, or constraints (e.g., TTT instability, prompt-dependent memory reading, benchmark diversity).

Ethical concerns are not fully addressed: ELViM uses YouTube tutorial videos without discussing consent, licensing, or compensation for human annotators; using Gemini-2.5-Pro for annotation raises terms-of-use questions.

The memory-discarding procedure (cosine similarity with the next token) may break temporal order by discarding tokens in the middle without re-ordering, but this is not analyzed or ablated against merging with TTT_MEM.
The two-stage training scheme's benefit is modest (0.2–0.4% on long benchmarks), and the necessity of freezing TTT_MEM in Stage 2 is not thoroughly justified.

The paper claims 'processes over 3-hour videos' but does not report a specific 3-hour video result; the maximum evaluated duration is about 92 minutes in ELViM, and LVBench/VideoEvalPro are described as several hours without a per-duration breakdown.

strengths: The paper introduces a novel use of test-time training (TTT) as a streaming memory mechanism for long-duration audio-visual video understanding, with a well-motivated TTT_MEM layer, long-span prediction objective, two-stage training scheme, and modality-aware memory reader (Sections 3.1-3.3).

Empirical results are strong and consistently support the central claims: video-SALMONN S outperforms streaming and non-streaming baselines on Video-MME long, LVBench, VideoEvalPro, and ELViM (Table 1), with controlled comparisons using the same Qwen3-VL 8B backbone and training data.

The ablation studies are thorough, isolating token downsampling, TTT variants, stage-2 training, memory reading, memory size, frame count, long-span prediction, deepstack embeddings, and prediction spans (Tables 2, 8, 9, 10; Figures 6-8).

The ELViM benchmark is a useful contribution: it targets long-term procedural memory under streaming constraints, uses a careful pipeline with timestamp filtering, LLM filtering, and human collation, and includes statistics and examples (Appendix A-B).

Reproducibility is reasonably supported by detailed model, training, and evaluation configurations, including architecture, hyperparameters, datasets, hardware, and runtime/FLOP statistics (Sections 5, 6.3, Appendices D-F).
The impact statement responsibly discusses privacy, bias, compute, and mitigation strategies.
weaknesses: The 'SOTA' framing is stronger than the evaluation: the main comparison includes only two streaming memory baselines (similarity merging and PEMF) plus Qwen3-VL and video-SALMONN 2+, while many recent streaming methods discussed in related work (e.g., ReKV, StreamMem, InfiniPot-V, Flash-VStream, Dispider) are not evaluated under the same protocol.

ELViM is generated and filtered with Gemini-2.5-Pro and Qwen3-VL-8B, which may introduce LLM-specific biases; human performance, inter-annotator agreement, and detailed annotation quality metrics are not reported.

The long-span prediction objective is heuristic: the default T=2 and maximum T=32 chunks cover only minutes rather than hours, and there is no theoretical analysis of fast-weight memory capacity, interference, or forgetting.

The modality-aware memory reading mechanism adds complexity, and the exact per-layer KV budget may exceed the stated average M because non-multimodal tokens are added back; the cost of prompt-dependent reprocessing across many streaming queries is not analyzed.
No code or model weights are released, and no reproducibility checklist is provided, which limits independent verification of the TTT_MEM and memory-reading implementation.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations section and does not ablate the decision to bypass TTT_MEM for audio, despite the audio-visual framing; minor inconsistencies also appear (e.g., abstract 15% vs. conclusion 14.2% on ELViM, and '3-7%' does not cover all non-streaming comparisons).
